title: Heterostructure-engineered diamond-graphene composites for high-performance and stable electromagnetic wave absorption

paper_content.abstract: Designing electromagnetic wave absorbing (EWA) materials that simultaneously deliver strong attenuation and withstand harsh environments remains a major challenge due to long-standing trade-offs between dielectric performance and structural robustness. Here, we report a heterostructured diamond-graphene composite synthesized under moderate high-pressure and high-temperature conditions, in which multilayer graphene is embedded within a nanodiamond framework through covalently bonded interfaces. This architecture enables modulation of the sp3/sp2 hybridization ratios, yielding tunable dielectric responses, improved impedance matching, and multiple, synergistic energy-dissipation pathways. The optimized composite achieves a minimum reflection loss of -60 dB and an effective absorption bandwidth of 4.0 GHz. Simultaneously, the material exhibits exceptional environmental tolerance, including high thermal stability, reliable absorption at high temperatures, large fracture toughness, and enhanced corrosion resistance, which originates from the mechanically interlocked diamond/graphene networks and chemically stable carbon interfaces. Our results establish a scalable heterointerface-engineering strategy for constructing multifunctional carbon architectures that unify strong microwave attenuation with outstanding thermal, mechanical, and chemical durability, offering a promising platform for next-generation EWA materials suitable for harsh or demanding environments.
paper_content.introduction:
The rapid advancement of wireless communication technology has led to a substantial increase in electromagnetic radiation in the environment1–3. This growing pollution poses potential human health risks from prolonged exposure and causing serious electromagnetic interference due to strong induction effects4,5. To mitigate these issues, ideal electromagnetic wave absorbing (EWA) materials should be lightweight, highly efficient, thin, and capable of operating across a broad frequency range6. Conventional EWA materials, such as ferrites, metals, conductive polymers, and dielectrics materials, have been used to reduce reflection and radiation7,8. However, their practical applications are limited by issues like impedance mismatch, narrow bandwidth, single loss mechanism, and poor resistance to corrosion or oxidation9. These limitations reduce their effectiveness and durability, particularly under demanding environmental conditions6. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop advanced EWA materials that offer both high absorption efficiency and strong environmental stability.

Carbon materials—including graphene, carbon nanotubes, and carbon dots—have garnered considerable attention for electromagnetic wave absorption because of their low density, tunable electrical properties, and cost-effective synthesis10,11. Unfortunately, single-component carbon nanomaterials often exhibit poor impedance matching and insufficient energy attenuation, primarily attributed to their excessively high electrical conductivity and the absence of diverse loss mechanisms12-14. To overcome these shortcomings, various strategies such as multicomponent design or element doping have been explored to optimize electromagnetic parameters and enhance energy dissipation by regulating composition, interface architecture, and defect density14–17. Despite notable progress, existing carbon-based composites still face persistent challenges, including weak filler-matrix interactions, non-uniform dispersion, and limited resistance to oxidation and corrosion under extreme environmental conditions6,18. To address these limitations, the integration of diamond and graphene via covalent bonding presents a promising avenue19–24. Diamond contributes exceptional chemical and thermal stability25, while graphene imparts high electrical conductivity and facilitates efficient charge transport23,24. The formation of robust covalent interfaces between these two components maybe improve impedance matching, introduce multiple energy dissipation pathways26, and enhance mechanical robustness. This synergistic design strategy offers a pathway toward high-performance EWA materials capable of withstanding harsh operating environments.

Here we report an efficient strategy for the fabrication of heterostructured diamond composites engineered within a diamond matrix for designing high-performance EWA materials under moderate pressure and temperature conditions27. The material consists of multilayer graphene domains embedded in nanodiamond (ND) matrices, with covalently bonded interfaces. The optimized material shows a maximum effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 4.0 GHz at 2.7 mm and a minimum reflection loss (RL) of -60 dB at 3.0 mm, while maintaining stable performance across a broad temperature range (300–973 K). The composite also exhibits a fracture toughness of 16.8 MPa·m1/2, a Vickers hardness of 41.9 GPa, an oxidation onset temperature of 1145 K, a corrosion potential of -0.210 V, and a low corrosion current density of 10-6 A/cm2. These findings provide a promising strategy for designing multifunctional EWA materials, offering new possibilities for advanced applications in harsh environments such as aerospace, military systems, and advanced electronics.
paper_content.results:
Design and preparation of diamond composites

Figure 1a illustrates the synthesis route for the diamond composites (DC). ND particles with an average diameter of ~5 nm were first annealed at 1200 oC, inducing partial graphitization and forming fullerene-wrapped diamond nanostructures. These pre-graphitized NDs were then used as precursors for high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment. Under conditions of 7.0 GPa and 1100-1300 oC, three composite samples were obtained, each exhibiting a distinctive hybrid microstructure in which multilayer graphene fragments are coherently embedded with a diamond matrix (Fig. 1b). For clarity, the products synthesized at 1100 oC, 1200 oC, and 1300 oC are denoted DC-1, DC-2, DC-3, respectively. A key distinction of the present diamond–graphene composites is the substantially reduced synthesis pressure enabled by the pre-graphitization strategy. Unlike Diaphene, which requires ~12 GPa, the composites form at 7 GPa while retaining comparable mechanical properties. This reduction arises from an interface-mediated phase transformation pathway introduced by the pre-formed sp² carbon shell. During HPHT treatment, the graphitic layers accommodate compressive strain through bond rehybridization and interlayer sliding, redistributing local stress and lowering the effective barrier for sp²→sp³ reconstruction at the diamond surface47–49. In addition, the intimate contact between graphene and nanodiamond provides coherent interfacial templates that facilitate localized nucleation of sp³ bonds, bypassing bulk diffusion-controlled transformation50. These cooperative effects, such as stress accommodation, reduced nucleation barriers, and constrained carbon migration, shift the transformation from a pressure-dominated bulk process to an interface-controlled reconstruction mechanism, enabling hybrid diamond–graphene architectures to form under milder conditions. Structurally, both materials feature interconnected ND grains bridged by few-to multi-layer graphene domains, forming continuous sp²-sp³ covalent interfaces that promote efficient load transfer and improve toughness. Consistently, the DC composites exhibit Vickers hardness values ranging from 41.9 to 51.7 GPa and fracture toughness spanning 10.5 to 16.8 MPa·m1/2, closely matching those of Diaphene.

Beyond mechanical robustness, the covalently bonded diamond/graphene interface imparts a suite of advantageous properties, summarized in Fig. 1c. Notably, DC-3 exhibits an oxidation onset temperature of 1145 K, exceeding those of natural diamond, nanopolycrystalline diamond (NPD), and Diaphene. The thermal conductivity of 3.5 W·m-1·K-1 highlights the strong phonon scattering inherent to the nanostructured architecture, while the corrosion potential of -0.210 V. reflects enhanced electrochemical stability. Most importantly, the optimized composite delivers excellent electromagnetic wave absorption, with a RL of -60 dB and an EAB of 4.0 GHz, positioning it among the leading carbon-based absorbers capable of operating under extreme environmental conditions.

Microstructure and dielectric properties

To examine the microstructure of the diamond composites, we performed scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). High-resolution high-angle annular dark field-STEM (HAADF-STEM) images (Figs. 2a-b) reveal a ND matrix embedded with multilayer graphene domains. Magnified images reveal an atomic-scale continuity between graphene and diamond (Figs. 2c-d), providing direct evidence of covalently bonded sp2-sp3 interfaces21 rather than simple van der Waals contact. Carbon K-edge electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) mapping acquired across the interfacial region (Fig. 2e) further confirms mixed bonding character: graphene domains exhibit a prominent π* at 284 eV, whereas diamond grains show the σ* feature at 292 eV19. These observations demonstrate the formation of covalently bridged diamond/graphene heterointerfaces throughout the composite. X-ray diffraction patterns (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 1a) display the coexistence of broad graphitic (002) peak and characteristic diamond reflections at (111), (220) and (311). Rietveld refinement yields diamond phase fractions of 78.3%, 74.1%, and 63.9% for DC-1, DC-2, and DC-3, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 2), consistent with progressive graphitization at higher synthesis temperatures. Despite the HAADF-STEM observation of multilayer graphene, no discernible 2D band is detected in Raman spectra (Supplementary Fig. 1b), likely due to interfacial bonding, local lattice distortions, and defect formation that disrupt the double-resonance process28,29. The decreasing ID/IG ratios and enhanced sp2 signal in XPS (Supplementary Fig. 1c) corroborate the formation of interconnected diamond/graphene networks.

Electromagnetic parameters (Fig. 2g and Supplementary Fig. 3) indicate that dielectric loss in the DC composites originates from the combined contributions of conduction loss and multiscale polarization mechanisms. Abundance sp³/sp² heterojunctions introduces strong interfacial polarization due to the conductivity contrast, while defect-rich graphene layers support dipolar relaxation30. Graphitic networks further facilitate electron hopping and conduction loss17, increasing the magnitude of ε′′ while maintaining the frequency-dependent trends observed in ND. The prominent loss peaks near 6-8 GHz and 11-15 GHz are attributed primarily to interfacial and defect-mediated relaxation associated with the diamond-rich matrix, explaining why graphene incorporation enhances the overall dielectric loss but does not shift the relaxation frequencies31. Cole-Cole plots demonstrate multiple relaxation semicircles for all DC samples (Supplementary Fig. 4), in contrast to the simpler profile of graphene powder, reflecting a more heterogeneous distribution of dipolar species and interfacial polarization sites. DC-2 and DC-3 show broader and more numerous semicircles than either ND or CVD diamond, consistent with their richer population of sp2-sp3 interfaces. Quantitative analysis of conductive (εc″) and polarization (εp″) components (Fig. 2h) further reveals that conduction loss dominates below 4 GHz, whereas polarization loss becomes the principal attenuation mechanism at 4–18 GHz. For DC-3, εc″ accounts for ~77% of total ε″ at 3 GHz, but decreases to 24% at 11 GHz and 15% at 14 GHz, accompanied by a corresponding increase in polarization contributions (Fig. 2j and Supplementary Fig. 5). Magnetic loss is negligible for all sample, as evidenced by the nearly uniform complex permeability (Supplementary Fig. 3), confirming the nonmagnetic nature of carbon-based materials. Instead, impedance matching is strongly modulated by the sp³/sp² ratio. As the diamond fraction decreases with increasing synthesis temperature, impedance matching improves. For DC-3 (63.9% sp3), the majority of impedance values fall within the optimal 0.8-1.2 window (Fig. 2i), enabling efficient microwave coupling and broadband attenuation.

Impact of heterostructure engineering on dielectric properties

The advantages of heterostructure engineering are further demonstrated by the enhanced EWA performance. The calculated RL and EAB of all DC composites and the ND precursor were calculated from transmission line theory6:

Zin =Z’−jZ’’=Z0 √μr/εr tanh[j(2πfd/c)√μr εr] (1)

RL (dB)=20•log |(Zin -Z0)/(Zin +Z0)| (2)

where Zin is the input impedance, d is the absorber thickness, c is the speed of light, f is the microwave frequency, and Z0 is the characteristic impedance of free space. To elucidate how interfacial defect sites and diamond grain size modulate the dielectric response, we carried out first-principles calculations. Two representative diamond/graphene interface models were constructed: one defect-free and one containing vacancy defects (Figs. 3a-b). Their calculated dielectric constants and impedance matching coefficients are presented in Fig. 3c. Due to the intrinsic non-magnetic nature of carbon-based materials, the complex magnetic permeability was set to 1.0, and the impedance matching coefficient Z was evaluated accordingly32:

Z =|Zin/Z0| =|√μr/εr tanh(j(2πfd/c)√μr εr)| (3)

Incorporation of the calculated dielectric parameters into the impedance model shows that the defective interface yields a matching coefficient closer to unity at a thickness of 1.0 mm, indicating that vacancy defects at the heterointerfaces promote improved impedance matching and thereby enhance EWA performance. Defective sites at the diamond-graphene interface serve as pivotal centers for energy dissipation, as the local chemical heterogeneity induces both permanent dipoles and charge‐trapping states that amplify dielectric loss. The presence of dangling bonds and sp³–sp² transitions creates a distribution of dipole moments and relaxation times, which manifest as broadened and overlapping semicircles in the Cole–Cole representation (Supplementary Fig. 4), thereby elevating ε″. To further assess the role of structural length scale, we constructed additional interface models with systematically varied diamond grain sizes, labeled size-1, size-2, and size-3 (Figs. 3d-f). The resulting complex dielectric constants are presented in Fig. 3g. Below 12 GHz, the largest-grain model (size-3) exhibits the highest real permittivity, reflecting enhanced charge-storage capability. However, above 12 GHz, its permittivity decreases sharply and becomes lower than that of the smaller-grain models. The imaginary permittivity (Fig. 3h) increases monotonically with grain size, indicating progressively stronger dielectric loss. Despite this trend, the impedance matching coefficients (Fig. 3i) reveal that the smallest-grain model achieves the most favorable matching at 1.0 mm thickness. This suggests that reduced grain size facilitates better wave penetration and balanced energy dissipation. The first-principles results demonstrate that both interfacial defect chemistry and grain-size modulation play decisive roles in optimizing EWA behavior. These insights highlight the critical importance of microstructural design in enabling next-generation diamond/graphene absorbers with tunable and superior electromagnetic attenuation performance.

EWA performance

In the ND precursor, the high content of sp3-hybridized carbon limits electron transport and suppresses polarization-relaxation processes, resulting in poor microwave absorption (Figs. 4a-c). As the synthesis temperature increases, the sp2 carbon content rises, thereby modifying the dielectric properties and electrical conductivity of the composites (Supplementary Fig. 6). These structural and compositional transitions directly influence EWA performance, as reflected by the evolution of RLmin, EABmax, and optimal thickness (Figs. 4d-f). Specifically, DC-1 exhibits an RLmin of -12.5 dB with an EABmax of 2.6 GHz at 6.0 mm (Supplementary Figs. 7g-i). DC-2 shows a marked improvement with an RLmin of -30.0 dB and an EABmax of 3.6 GHz at 2.8 mm (Supplementary Figs. 7m-o). Notably, DC-3 delivers the strongest performance, enabled by its optimized graphene content. It achieves an EABmax of 4.0 GHz and an RLmin of -42.3 dB at 2.7 mm, and further reaches an ultradeep RLmin of -60 dB at only 3.0 mm (Fig. 4f).

To further interpret the absorption behavior, impedance matching was analyzed using the impedance-matching coefficient Z33:

Z =|Zin/Z0| =|√μr/εr tanh(j(2πfd/c)√μr εr)| (4)

when Z = 1.0, incident microwaves enter the absorber with minimal reflection. Achieving Z values close to 1.0 over a broad frequency range is critical to ensure maximum electromagnetic wave entry into the absorber. Although graphene is highly conductive and ND is insulating—conditions that usually lead to poor impedance matching—the formation of covalently bonded sp²-sp³ interfaces introduces heterogeneous microstructures containing defects and interfaces of varying dimensions19. These features suppress the overall conductivity and significantly improve impedance matching. As shown in Figs. 3g-i, DC-1 and DC-2 maintain Z values mostly above 1.2, whereas DC-3 exhibits a broad optimal matching region (Z = 0.8-1.2), consistent with its superior EWA performance. To elucidate the role of interfacial structures, ND and nanographene (NG) were mechanically mixed at ratios of 8:2, 7:3, and 6:4 and treated under the same HPHT conditions as DC-3 (Supplementary Fig. 8). The resulting composites (DG-1, DG-2, DG-3) showed progressively improved EWA performance with increasing NG content; however, all remained inferior to DC-3. For example, DG-3 achieves an RLmin of −55.7 dB at 4.5 mm and an EABmax of 3.3 GHz at 2.0 mm, whereas DC-3 reaches −60 dB at a smaller thickness of 3.0 mm and a broader EABmax of 4.0 GHz at 2.7 mm (~3.8 GHz at 2.0 mm). This disparity highlights that physical mixing produces heterogeneous, weakly bonded interfaces and discontinuous sp² domains, which hinder charge transport and degrade impedance matching26. In contrast, the pre-graphitization strategy of the DC composites yields continuous covalent sp²-sp³ networks, enabling efficient conduction and polarization losses that result in superior EWA capability. Importantly, impedance matching alone is insufficient. The absorber must also possess strong energy-attenuation capability to dissipate incident microwaves; otherwise, reflected energy from the backing layer may reemit into free space. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 9, DC-3 exhibits the highest attenuation coefficient, consistent with its elevated imaginary permittivity and enhanced dielectric loss behavior. Compared with state-of-the-art carbon-based and magnetic absorbers32-38 (Fig. 4j and Supplementary Table1), DC-3 achieves both an ultrahigh RLmin (-60 dB) and a broad EABmax of 4.0 GHz, placing it among the leading carbon-based EWA materials. Importantly, this degree of attenuation at such a small thickness surpasses many high-performance absorbers, which typically require 4-5 mm to achieve comparable suppression. The optimized sp²/sp³ hybrid architecture in DC-3 therefore provides an advantageous balance between minimal thickness, strong attenuation, and broadband absorption, underscoring its potential for lightweight and miniaturized electromagnetic shielding and stealth applications.

To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we analyzed both conduction and polarization contributions to dielectric loss (Fig. 4k). The highly conductive sp2-rich networks enhance conduction loss via efficient charge transport. Meanwhile, the numerous heterointerfaces create local electric-field gradients where electrons preferentially accumulate on the graphene side, intensifying interfacial polarization. Dielectric loss arises from two primary contributions—conduction loss and polarization loss. The internal architecture of the composites contains numerous heterogeneous diamond–graphene interfaces, at which electrons preferentially accumulate on the graphene side, thereby strengthening interfacial polarization and contributing to enhanced energy dissipation2. Defective and edge carbon atoms introduce permanent dipoles, supporting dipolar relaxation and further boosting dielectric loss. Overall, the integrated diamond-graphene structure enables strong conduction and interfacial polarization losses while maintaining favorable impedance matching, collectively yielding efficient and broadband microwave attenuation.

Serviceability in extreme environments

To assess the suitability of the DC composites for use under extreme environments, we examined their mechanical, thermal and chemical stability. Thermal transport measurements reveal that DC-3 exhibits a remarkably low thermal conductivity of 3.5 W·m-1·K-1 at room temperature (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 10). This strong insulating behavior arises from its nanostructured architecture, with diamond nanograins surrounded by abundant interfaces and defect-rich boundaries that strongly scatter phonons and charge carriers. The composite also displays excellent oxidation resistance, with an onset temperature of 1145 K, surpassing natural diamond, NPD, and Diaphene (Supplementary Fig. 11). This enhancement may originate from the sp³-sp² covalent interfaces19,20,24, where graphene layers act as an oxygen-blocking barrier and the diamond nanograins become energetically stable25. Moreover, interfacial stress and charge redistribution further reduce surface energy and suppress oxidative reactions21. The cooperative effect of these factors leads to the delayed onset of oxidation, demonstrating that interface engineering is an efficient strategy to improve the environmental tolerance of diamond-based composites. Fracture toughness and Vickers hardness were measured under a 9.8 N load (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 12). The DC samples show fracture toughness values of 10.5-16.8 MPa·m1/2, with Vickers hardness values of 51.7 ± 2.4 GPa (DC-1), 44.5 ± 3.1 GPa (DC-2), and 41.9 ± 1.5 GPa (DC-3). Flexural strength is critical for maintaining structural stability under mechanical loading, ensuring that EWA components preserve their geometry and performance during service. Although the flexural strength of DC-3 (20~60 MPa, as shown Supplementary Figs. 12-13) is lower than that of CVD diamond (350.7 MPa, as shown Supplementary Fig. 12e), it remains high for carbon-based composites39. However, the stress–strain curves exhibit pronounced non-brittle behavior (Supplementary Fig. 13), attributable to the diamond–multilayer graphene architecture. The graphene layers hinder crack propagation through crack bridging, interfacial sliding, and deflection, thereby suppressing catastrophic brittle fracture typical of monolithic diamond and ensuring adequate mechanical integrity for load-bearing or vibration-intensive electromagnetic applications.

Electrochemical corrosion resistance was evaluated in NaCl solution (Fig. 5c). DC-3 show a corrosion potential (Ecorr = -0.21 V) and a corrosion current density (Icorr < 10-6 A/cm2), indicating strong electrochemical passivation. The positive shift in Ecorr suggests that the composite acts as an anodic barrier, suppressing electron release and minimizing corrosion18. Bode impedance spectra (Fig. 5d) further demonstrate high |Z| values at low frequencies, confirming robust protection. This behavior correlates directly with the sp³/sp² ratio: the diamond matrix supplies chemical inertness, while sp2 domains promote charge delocalization and minimize local potential gradients. Excessive sp², however, increases surface reactivity, underscoring the need for an optimized hybrid ratio (Fig. 5e). Thus, an optimal balance between the two ensures both structural stability and electronic equilibrium at the interface22, effectively improving corrosion resistance through synergistic chemical passivation and charge delocalization. Finite element simulations of power-loss density (PLD) distribution (Fig. 5f) consistently show that DC-3 exhibits the most intense and spatially extensive PLD at 7 GHz (C-band), 11 GHz (X-band), and 15 GHz (Ku-band)11, directly reflecting its superior microwave attenuation capacity. High-temperature absorption measurements (Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. 14) demonstrate that DC-3 maintain stable microwave attenuation between 773-973 K. With increasing temperature, the permittivity decreases (Supplementary Fig. 15) and the optimal absorption thickness shifts toward larger thickness; at a fixed 3.2 mm thickness, the bandwidth gradually narrows35.

Although HPHT synthesis reliably produces covalently bonded sp³-sp² interfaces and high-performance composites, scale-up remains limited by the requirements of ultra-high pressure, high temperature, and high energy consumption. Strategies to reduce cost and improve throughput include tailoring precursor chemistry to lower transformation thresholds, adopting spark plasma sintering (SPS)40 or hot-pressing, and exploring hybrid HPHT-SPS approaches. In addition, emerging metal-catalyzed pathways, such as liquid Ga-, Ni-, or Cu-mediated formation of sp³-sp² interfaces41-46 offer promising alternative routes to large-scale production of covalently integrated carbon heterostructures. Overall, DC-3 combines high mechanical strength, low thermal conductivity, excellent oxidation and corrosion resistance, and stable high-temperature microwave absorption, making it a promising candidate for demanding aerospace, aviation, and high-performance engineering applications.

In summary, we have developed a diamond composite that combines efficient electromagnetic wave absorption with exceptional environmental tolerance by integrating multilayer graphene within a nanodiamond matrix through sp2-sp3 heterointerfaces. This engineered architecture enhances mechanical robustness, enables favorable impedance matching, and activates multiple energy-dissipation pathways, allowing the material to retain strong absorption performance even under extreme operating conditions. The optimized composite achieves a minimum reflection loss of −60 dB together with an effective absorption bandwidth of 4.0 GHz, outperforming many previously reported carbon-based absorbers. This heterointerface design strategy, combined with scalable fabrication route, provides a versatile framework for creating multifunctional and highly stable carbon-based EWA materials through controlled tuning of diamond and graphene domains. The demonstrated thermal, mechanical, and chemical durability further positions the composite as a compelling candidate for aerospace, marine, and advanced electronics applications, where reliable operation in harsh environments is essential.
paper_content.methods:
Sample preparation

Nanodiamond powers (99%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical technology Co., Ltd. The initial nanodiamonds were first annealed in air at 450 oC for 60 minutes to remove amorphous carbon and sp2-bonded carbons. Subsequently, the samples were dried under vacuum in a tube furnace at 1200 oC for 10 minutes to induce structural transformation. High-pressure high-temperature synthesis was conducted using a China-type cubic large-volume press system equipped with a custom-designed sample assembly. Temperature was monitored with type-C thermocouples, and pressure was estimated based on established calibration curves. The recovered samples were 13.5-14.0 mm in diameter and 1.5-2.0 mm in height.

Structural characterization

X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were performed using a Rigaku SmartLab diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation source (λ = 1.5406 Å). Phase composition and volume fractions were determined through Rietveld refinement analysis. Raman spectra were recorded at room temperature using a Horiba LabRAM HR Evolution system with a 532 nm excitation laser. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra were conducted on an ESCALAB 250 Xi system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to analyze elemental chemical states. Thin lamellae for transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were prepared via focused ion beam using a Helios G4 system. High-resolution TEM and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) images were acquired using a FEI Themis Z spherical aberration-corrected microscope operating at 300 kV. Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) was acquired to determine the bonding sates of the composites.

Electromagnet parameter measurement

The electromagnetic parameters of the composites were measured using a vector network analyzer (Agilent E5071C) in the frequency range of 1–18 GHz. For testing, the samples were fabricated into toroidal shapes with outer and inner diameters of 7.00 mm and 3.04 mm, respectively. The reflection loss (RL), effective absorption bandwidth (EAB), attenuation coefficient, and impedance matching coefficient were calculated using custom Python scripts and CST Microwave Studio software. Electrical resistivity (ρ) as a function of temperature was measured in the range of 2-300 K using the standard four-probe method with a Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS, Quantum Design Inc.). Platinum wires were affixed to the polished sample surface using silver paste to ensure good electrical contact. The electrical conductivity (σ) was calculated from the measured resistivity values according to the relation σ =1/ρ.

Corrosion resistance measurement

The electrochemical measurements were conducted to further evaluate the stability of DC samples. Bulk specimens were tested using Princeton VersaSTAT 4 electrochemical workstation, employing a of 3.5 % NaCl solution as the electrolyte and Ta saturated calomel electrode as the reference electrode. Electrochemical impedance (EIS) measurements were performed within the frequency range of 0.1–105 Hz with an amplitude of 10 mV. Tafel polarization curves were recorded over a potential range of -1 V to 1 V at a scan rate of 1 mV/s to determine the corrosion potential and the corrosion resistance of the samples.

High temperature microwave absorption testing

Microwave absorption performance at elevated temperatures was assessed using the waveguide method with a vector network analyzer (Ceyear 3672B) in the X-band frequency range. Samples were machined into rectangular parallelepipeds with dimensions of 22.86 mm × 10.16 mm × 1 mm to ensure compatibility with the waveguide system. The multiple synthesized samples were ground and consolidated using high-purity silica gel (SiO2·nH2O) to form specimens suitable. A controlled heating rate of 5 °C/min was applied, followed by a 10-minute isothermal holding period at each target temperature (773 K, 873 K, and 973 K) to ensure achieve thermal equilibrium prior to measurement. In addition, to exclude any potential influence of the high-purity silicone (a high transparency adhesive used for high-temperature microwave absorption measurement51) on the measurements, a control experiment was performed at 873 K, and its effect was found to be negligible (Supplementary Fig. 16).

Mechanical and thermal measurements

The standard Vickers hardness of samples was measured using a microhardness tester (KB5-BVZ) on polished surfaces. An applied load was maintained for a dwell time of 10 s. The Vickers hardness (Hv) was calculated using the equation: Hv = 1854.4F/L2, where F (N) is the applied load and L (μm) is the average diagonal length of the Vickers indentation. Five indentations were obtained at each to calculate an average hardness value. Fracture toughness (KIC) was determined from KIC = 0.016(E/Hv)0.5F/C1.5, where F (N) is the applied load, C (μm) is the average length of the radial cracks measured from the indent center, and E (1140 GPa) is Young’s modulus of diamond. The flexural strength of the synthesized samples was evaluated using a three-point bending test. The thermal stability of the samples was tested using a NETZSCH STA 449F3 system, with a heating rate of 5 K/min across a temperature range from 300 to 1473 K. The thermal diffusivity was determined using an LFA467HT HyperFlash system, with measurements conducted at intervals of 50 K from 300 to 800 K, and at least three data points collected at each temperature to ensure accuracy.

Numerical simulation

Power loss density (PLD) distributions were simulated using COMSOL Multiphysics®. To optimize computational efficiency, a simplified cubic model with dimensions of 6 mm × 6 mm × 4 mm was employed. Microwave excitation at frequencies of 7, 11, and 15 GHz was introduced along the z-axis from the top surface. Periodic boundary conditions were applied in both the x and y directions to emulate infinite lateral extension and reduce edge effects.

First-principles calculations

All calculations were performed using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) within the GGA-PBE framework and projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials. The 500 eV cutoff energy was used. Structural relaxation was conducted with a 10×3×1 k-point mesh until forces were below 0.02 eV/Å and energy convergence reached 10-6 eV. We constructed diamond/graphite heterostructures, then created a carbon vacancy model and 3, 6, 9-layer variants. Dielectric constants were computed after full optimization of all five systems.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
General Comment
The authors report on a composite composed entirely of carbon allotropes for EM wave absorption. The EWA performance
itself seems solid, with calculations done using trivially utilized methods. However, extensive improvements must be made
in revealing the role of the interfaces and individual materials inside the composite on the EWA properties, especially in
nanocomposites like this case where the combined materials are composed of the same element. (It is much easier to split
the role in a more ‘heterogeneous’ structure such as a graphene-polymer composite).
Comments
- Is the term ‘graphene’ fully appropriate in this study? It feels like terms such as ‘graphitic carbon’ would better suit in this
case.
- In the Raman data, show the full-range data to include the 2D peak regions. Also, add additional interpretations on the
graphitic structure based on the 2D peak region.
- In Figure 2h, the authors must discuss in detail the correlation between material chemistry and dielectric loss parameters,
and what types of vibrations at which dimensions (atomic? Molecular? Dipolar?) result in the dielectric properties observed
in the composite.
- For the imaginary permittivity (e’’) in Figure 2h, the pattern of nanodiamond (black lines) is similar to those of DC-1, DC-2,
and DC-3 (Especially for the peaks near 6-8 GHz and 11-15 GHz). It is understandable that the conductive graphitic sheets
contribute to the increased real permittivity (e’), but why does e’’ show a similar pattern bettwen DC-1, 2, 3 and nd? If the
graphene with sp2 carbon should contribute, it should add a different dielectric loss pattern compared to the sp3
nanodiamond.
- Add analyses based on Cole-Cole plots on the EWA performance and properties.
- I do not see any clear proof on the covalent bonding between and diamond. It is very important to reveal this, as the edge
bonding structure of diamond and graphene will highly differ depending on whether they are physically adjoined or
covalently bound together, which eventually influences the dielectric properties.
- Discuss the influence of defective sites at the interface between graphene and diamond, and how their chemical structure
and dipoles influence the EWA performance.
- In Figure 3j, authors must add comparison with state-of-the-art composites based on magnetic materials as well. Although
this paper is based on dielectric materials (carbons), the overall comparison still needs to include magnetic materials, as
they are the dominant EWA materials in the studies frequency range.
- I think that this composite could also be made and controlled by initially adding nanodiamonds and nanographenes
together and apply the HTHP process, which would create different interfaces. Discuss on this method in creating
composites and their EWA properties.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Carbon has many allotropes, and each one has greatly boosted technological progress and social development. This
diversity comes from carbon's ability to form sp, sp2, and sp3 hybridizations. Different hybridizations lead to stark differences
in physical and chemical properties. Recently, hybrid structures and composites combining diamond with graphite/graphene
have been developed. These materials integrate diamond's superhardness and the high electrical conductivity of
graphite/graphene, achieving unique property combinations that single allotropes cannot match, which is of great
significance for expanding the application scope of carbon materials. This type of novel carbon material is typically obtained
by using high pressure to induce phase transitions from sp2-hybridized carbon precursors to the sp3-hybridized diamond
phase. In this work, the authors reversed this process by inducing an sp³ to sp² transition under moderate high-pressure and
high-temperature conditions, resulting in the production of large-size diamond/graphene composites. These composites not
only exhibit superhardness and electrical conductivity but also show potential for electromagnetic wave-absorbing
applications. This study, demonstrating both timeliness and importance, is recommended for publication in Nature
Communications. Nevertheless, there are several issues that need to be addressed.
1. The authors are advised to supplement the structural characterization with detailed TEM observations focusing on the
interface between diamond and graphene. The authors should provide direct evidence to clarify the nature of the bonding at
the interface, determining the type of interaction—whether it is van der Waals or covalent. This clarification is crucial for
offering a structural explanation for the superior mechanical and microwave absorption performance.
2. Given the authors' recent report on synthesizing similar composite Diaphene [PNAS, 2024, 121.9: e2316580121], the
authors are expected to conduct a thorough comparison between this work and the Diaphene in three aspects: differences in
preparation methods, microstructural characteristics, and mechanical properties.
3. Regarding the microwave absorption performance of the samples, the optimal sample achieves a minimum reflection loss
of -61.47dB at a thickness of 5.5mm, which is relatively thick. Generally, studies typically report data up to a thickness of
5mm. The material shows nearly -60dB performance at 3.5mm, which is comparable to previously reported carbon-based
microwave absorption materials and offers a certain thickness advantage. It is suggested that the authors select this data
point as the optimal RL value for specific analysis.
4. In the discussion of serviceability in extreme environments, hardness may not be the most critical mechanical property for
electromagnetic wave absorption materials. It is recommended that the authors provide additional mechanical property
indicators such as fracture toughness, and bending strength.
Additionally, the DC-3 sample's initial oxidation temperature of 1145 K surpasses that of natural diamond and NPD, and
even exceeds the previously reported Diaphene. Further comparative analysis and discussion are needed to elaborate on
this aspect.
5. There are several minor issues in the paper that need to be addressed:
There is a discrepancy between the sample dimensions mentioned in the synthesis method and those used in the high-
temperature microwave absorption tests. The recovered samples are described as having a diameter of 13.5-14.0mm and a
height of 1.5-2.0mm, whereas the samples for microwave absorption testing are rectangular parallelepipeds with dimensions
of 22.86mm × 10.16mm × 1mm.
The Raman fitting results in Fig. 2f and Fig. S1b are inconsistent.
There is a spelling error in the word "hardness" at line 210.
The horizontal axis label in Fig. S1c contains a spelling error.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript titled "Heterostructure-Engineered Diamond-Graphene Composites for High-Performance and Stable
Electromagnetic Wave Absorption" presents a systematic study on the synthesis, characterization, and electromagnetic
wave absorption (EWA) performance of heterostructured diamond-graphene composites. This work addresses critical
limitations of conventional carbon-based EWA materials, such as poor impedance matching and insufficient environmental
resilience, but several core academic questions require further clarification. Here are some specific comments for the
authors:
1. The optimized composite (DC-3) achieves a minimum reflection loss of -61.47 dB, yet the supplementary Table 1
compares the material with other carbon-based absorbers but does not include data on the thickness corresponding to the
minimum reflection loss of these reference materials. How does the thickness of DC-3 (5.5 mm for -61.47 dB) compare to
that of the referenced materials when achieving their respective minimum reflection loss values, and what impact does this
thickness difference have on practical application potential?
2. The authors mention that the incoherent interface between diamond and graphene enhances impedance matching, but
they do not elaborate on the specific mechanism by which the incoherent interface regulates the impedance matching
coefficient. What is the relationship between the structural features of the incoherent interface (e.g., grain size of the ND,
interface defect density, lattice mismatch) and the impedance matching performance, and is there experimental or simulation
evidence to support this relationship? A theoretical simulation would be helpful to elucidate the underline mechanism.
3. The electrical conductivity of the DC samples increases with decreasing sp³ content, as shown in Fig. 2i, but the
manuscript does not discuss how the change in electrical conductivity specifically affects the conduction loss mechanism of
electromagnetic waves. How to quantitatively distinguish the contribution of conduction loss from other loss mechanisms
(e.g., interfacial polarization loss, dipole polarization loss) in the total dielectric loss of the composites?
4. The corrosion potential of DC-3 is -0.210 V, and the corrosion current density is less than 10⁻⁶ A/cm², indicating good
corrosion resistance. But the manuscript does not explain why the corrosion resistance of DC-1 (with higher sp³ content) is
slightly better than that of DC-2 and DC-3, as suggested by the Nyquist plots. What is the intrinsic relationship between
sp³/sp² content and the corrosion resistance mechanism of the composites?
5. The high-temperature electromagnetic wave absorption performance of DC-3 is stable between 773 K and 973 K, but the
absorption bandwidth decreases slightly with increasing temperature. The manuscript attributes this to temperature-
dependent hopping conductivity and dipole polarization, but there is no experimental data on the change of dielectric
parameters (ε', ε'') with temperature. What are the variations of complex permittivity and permeability of DC-3 at different high
temperatures (773 K, 873 K, 973 K), and how do these variations explain the change in absorption bandwidth?
6. The manuscript proposes that the heterostructure design of diamond-graphene composites provides a new strategy for
multifunctional electromagnetic wave absorbing materials, but it does not discuss the scalability and cost of the moderate
high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) synthesis method. What challenges exist in scaling up the HPHT preparation
process for industrial production, and are there potential improvements to reduce the synthesis cost while maintaining
material performance?
7. The author should provide a more updated review of literatures with covalent bonded sp3-sp2 carbon interfaces, which
could be catalyzed by metal such as liquid gallium, nickel or copper.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-Point Response to the Reviewers’ Comments
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their careful reviews and constructive
suggestions, which have significantly improved the clarity and quality of our work. We
believe that the revised manuscript and this response letter fully address the reviewers’
comments. Below, we provide detailed point-by-point responses. For clarity, the
reviewers’ comments are shown in black, our replies in blue, and the corresponding
manuscript revisions are marked in red.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
General Comment: The authors report on a composite composed entirely of carbon
allotropes for EM wave absorption. The EWA performance itself seems solid, with
calculations done using trivially utilized methods. However, extensive improvements
must be made in revealing the role of the interfaces and individual materials inside the
composite on the EWA properties, especially in nanocomposites like this case where
the combined materials are composed of the same element. (It is much easier to split
the role in a more ‘heterogeneous’ structure such as a graphene-polymer composite).
Reply: We sincerely thank you for your detailed comments and valuable
suggestions, which have been very helpful in improving the quality of our manuscript.
In response to the comments regarding the role of interfacial structures and the
individual components within the composite in determining the EWA properties, we
have incorporated additional experimental results and theoretical analyses to establish
a clearer correlation between the structural characteristics and the EWA properties.
Please refer to our detailed point-by-point responses below for further clarification.
1. Is the term ‘graphene’ fully appropriate in this study? It feels like terms such as
‘graphitic carbon’ would better suit in this case.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. In our study, the term
“graphene” was used to describe multilayer, sp²-bonded carbon structures that formed
within the diamond matrix during high-pressure, high-temperature processing. As
shown in Fig. R1, these layers exhibit (002) diffraction peak and Raman features (G
and D bands) of graphitic carbons, as confirmed by XRD, XPS and Raman analyses.
To further clearly characterize the microstructure, we have conducted high-angle
annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM)
measurements. Fig. R2 shows the HAADF-STEM images of the DC-3 sample, in which
diamond (D) and graphene (G) nanodomains are clearly distinguished. However, we
agree that these carbon layers are not ideal monolayer graphene but rather graphitic
domains with multilayer structures. To ensure accuracy and consistency, we have
revised the manuscript to refer to them as “multilayer graphene” where appropriate.
This clarification more accurately reflects their structural characteristics.
(a) X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern. (b) Raman spectra (532 nm excitation). (c) X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) pattern.
Fig. R2. Microstructures of the DC-3 sample. (a) High-resolution HAADF-STEM
image, where a diamond (D) matrix embedded with multilayer graphene (G) sheets. (b)
Magnified HAADF-STEM image of the white-boxed region in a, revealing an
atomically covalent interface between graphene and diamond. (c, d) Additional high-
magnification HAADF-STEM images exhibiting multilayer graphene. (e) HAADF-
STEM image showing multiple diamond/graphene interfaces. (f) Carbon K-edge EELS
spectra extracted from the surface-scan region marked by white dashed box in e.
2. In the Raman data, show the full-range data to include the 2D peak regions. Also,
2
add additional interpretations on the graphitic structure based on the 2D peak region.
Reply: Thank you very much for your valuable comments. Following your
suggestion, we show the full-range Raman spectra, including the 2D peak region, as
shown in Fig. R3. Although the HAADF-STEM images confirm the presence of
multilayer graphene (see Fig. R2), the 2D peak is not evident in the Raman spectra of
our samples, unlike the case of graphene sample. This absence can be attributed to
several factors. First, the strong interaction and bonding between graphene and diamond
at the incoherent interfaces may distort the π–π* electronic structure of graphene,
thereby suppressing the resonance conditions required for the 2D band. Second,
structural defects, lattice distortions, and partial sp³ hybridization introduced during
high-pressure, high-temperature synthesis can significantly reduce the intensity or even
eliminate the 2D peak. These combined effects result in an undetectable 2D peak,
despite the confirmed presence of multilayer graphene in the composite.
We have updated Fig. R3 into the revised manuscript as Supplementary Fig. 1b,
and have revised accordingly in the revised manuscript: “Despite the HAADF-STEM
observation of multilayer graphene, no discernible 2D band is detected in Raman
spectra (Supplementary Fig. 1b), likely due to interfacial bonding, local lattice
distortions, and defect formation that disrupt the double-resonance process28,29.” (Page
7, Lines 14–17)
Fig. R3. Raman spectra of the DC composites and ND precursors. The Raman
spectrum of graphene powder is shown for comparison.
3. In Figure 2h, the authors must discuss in detail the correlation between material
chemistry and dielectric loss parameters, and what types of vibrations at which
dimensions (atomic? Molecular? Dipolar?) result in the dielectric properties observed
in the composite.
expanded the discussion to clarify the correlation between material chemistry and the
observed dielectric loss parameters, as well as the nature and scale of the associated
polarization and vibration mechanisms.
In our diamond composites, the dielectric loss primarily originates from
conduction loss and polarization loss, both of which are strongly influenced by the
material’s chemical composition and heterostructure. The incorporation of sp²-bonded
multi-layer graphene within the sp³-bonded diamond matrix creates numerous
heterointerfaces, defects, and localized charge accumulation sites. These structural and
chemical features lead to several distinct polarization mechanisms operating at different
length scales:
Molecular or dipolar polarization: The presence of defects, vacancies, and
functional groups within the graphitic domains introduces dipoles that align with the
applied electromagnetic field, generating relaxation-type dielectric losses.
Interfacial polarization: At the nanoscale, the large number of diamond/graphitic
interfaces leads to charge accumulation due to conductivity contrast, resulting in
significant interfacial polarization and energy dissipation.
Conduction loss: The graphitic networks facilitate electron hopping and migration
under the alternating field, further enhancing dielectric loss.
The degree of graphitization directly affects the electrical conductivity and
interfacial density, which in turn modulate both ε′ (energy storage) and ε″ (energy
dissipation). As shown in Fig. R4, increasing sp² content enhances dielectric loss
through improved charge transport and intensified interfacial polarization.
We have added Fig. R4 into the revised manuscript as Fig. 2g, and added detailed
discussions in the manuscript: “Electromagnetic parameters (Fig. 2g and
Supplementary Fig. 3) indicate that dielectric loss in the DC composites originates from
the combined contributions of conduction loss and multiscale polarization mechanisms.
Abundance sp³/sp² heterojunctions introduces strong interfacial polarization due to the
conductivity contrast, while defect-rich graphene layers support dipolar relaxation30.”
(Page 7, Lines 19–22; Page 8, Line 1)
Fig. R4. The complex permittivity of DC, graphene, and diamond. (a) The real part
of the complex permittivity. (b) The imaginary part of the complex permittivity. (c) The
tangent value of complex permittivity.
4
4. For the imaginary permittivity (ε’’) in Figure 2h, the pattern of nanodiamond (black
lines) is similar to those of DC-1, DC-2, and DC-3 (Especially for the peaks near 6-8
GHz and 11-15 GHz). It is understandable that the conductive graphitic sheets
contribute to the increased real permittivity (ε’), but why does ε’’ show a similar pattern
between DC-1, 2, 3 and nd? If the graphene with sp2 carbon should contribute, it should
add a different dielectric loss pattern compared to the sp3 nanodiamond.
Reply: We thank the referee for the excellent question. To address this issue, we
performed additional experiments and compared the complex permittivity of the DC
composites, graphene, ND precursors and CVD diamond in the 2-18 GHz range (See
Fig. R4). For sp2 graphene, conduction loss is the dominant dielectric loss mechanism
due to its delocalized π-electron system, complemented by defect/dipolar polarization
(defects or functional groups) and interfacial polarization (stacked or agglomerated
graphene layers). Thus, the incorporation of graphene increases the overall ε′ and ε″
intensity (ε″ ∝ σ/ω) through improved electrical conductivity, but without shifting the
characteristic relaxation frequencies because GHz frequencies are far below graphene’s
intrinsic plasmonic range (THz).
For ND precursors synthesized via the detonation method, their surfaces inevitably
contain a certain amount of sp2 carbon, as evidenced by the Raman spectrum (Fig. R1b).
These surface-rich structure leads to interfacial polarization between sp3 core and
disordered sp2 shell and dipolar relaxation from surface functional groups. In contrast,
CVD diamond exhibits extremely low dielectric loss across 2-18 GHz due to its
electrically insulating nature, where ε″ primarily arises from dipolar relaxation related
to intrinsic defects, impurity-induced dipoles, and grain boundary polarization.
Therefore, in the 2–18 GHz range, the main dielectric loss mechanism is not
intrinsic plasmon resonance of sp2 graphene, but rather interfacial polarization and
dipolar relaxation caused by lattice defects, surface functional groups, and
diamond/graphene interfaces. These relaxation processes occur at similar time scales in
both ND, graphene and DC composites, leading to comparable ε″ peak patterns. The
presence of graphene increases ε″ intensity but does not shift the peak positions.
We have updated Fig. R4 into the revised manuscript as Fig. 2g, and have revised
accordingly in the revised manuscript: “Graphitic networks further facilitate electron
hopping and conduction loss17, increasing the magnitude of ε′′ while maintaining the
frequency-dependent trends observed in ND. The prominent loss peaks near 6-8 GHz
and 11-15 GHz are attributed primarily to interfacial and defect-mediated relaxation
associated with the diamond-rich matrix, explaining why graphene incorporation
enhances the overall dielectric loss but does not shift the relaxation frequencies31.”
(Page 8, Lines 1-5)
5. Add analyses based on Cole-Cole plots on the EWA performance and properties.
Reply: Thank you very much for your valuable suggestions. We sincerely
apologize for the oversight in our previous work, as Cole-Cole plots were inadvertently
omitted and has now been added in Fig. R5. The Cole–Cole plots of the DC samples,
nanodiamond (ND), and CVD diamond reveal multiple relaxation semicircles,
suggesting the presence of several distinct relaxation processes. In contrast, graphene
powder exhibits fewer semicircular features, indicating a reduced number of relaxation
5
mechanisms, thereby confirming that polarization losses are primarily associated with
the DC and diamond-based samples. Moreover, the Cole–Cole profiles of DC samples,
ND, and CVD diamond display markedly different relaxation characteristics, reflecting
variations in their dielectric loss behavior. The DC-3 sample exhibits a series of
overlapping semicircles with larger diameters and broader dispersion, indicative of
multiple relaxation processes and pronounced interfacial or dipolar polarization effects.
By comparison, the ND and CVD diamond samples show fewer and smaller semicircles,
implying a limited number of active relaxation pathways and weaker polarization
strength. The enlarged and more numerous relaxation semicircles observed in DC-2 and
DC-3 correspond to higher ε″ values over a broader frequency range, signifying
enhanced energy dissipation and greater dielectric loss. These findings suggest that DC-
3 possesses a more heterogeneous polarization environment, likely arising from
complex defect states and interfacial polarization, which collectively contribute to its
superior dielectric loss performance relative to ND.
We have added Fig. R5 into the revised manuscript as Supplementary Fig. 4, and
added detailed discussions in the revised manuscript: “Cole-Cole plots demonstrate
multiple relaxation semicircles for all DC samples (Supplementary Fig. 4), in contrast
to the simpler profile of graphene powder, reflecting a more heterogeneous distribution
of dipolar species and interfacial polarization sites. DC-2 and DC-3 show broader and
more numerous semicircles than either ND or CVD diamond, consistent with their

Reply: We are grateful for your kind comments. The defective sites at the
graphene–diamond interface significantly influence the EWA performance. We

magnitude and broader bandwidth of microwave attenuation. Thus, the defect-rich

As shown in Fig. R9, increasing the NG content enhances the EWA performance of the

Carbon has many allotropes, and each one has greatly boosted technological
progress and social development. This diversity comes from carbon's ability to form sp,
sp2, and sp3 hybridizations. Different hybridizations lead to stark differences in physical
and chemical properties. Recently, hybrid structures and composites combining
diamond with graphite/graphene have been developed. These materials integrate
diamond's superhardness and the high electrical conductivity of graphite/graphene,
achieving unique property combinations that single allotropes cannot match, which is
of great significance for expanding the application scope of carbon materials. This type
of novel carbon material is typically obtained by using high pressure to induce phase
transitions from sp2-hybridized carbon precursors to the sp3-hybridized diamond phase.
In this work, the authors reversed this process by inducing an sp³ to sp² transition under
moderate high-pressure and high-temperature conditions, resulting in the production of
large-size diamond/graphene composites. These composites not only exhibit
superhardness and electrical conductivity but also show potential for electromagnetic
wave-absorbing applications. This study, demonstrating both timeliness and importance,
is recommended for publication in Nature Communications. Nevertheless, there are
several issues that need to be addressed.
Reply: We are profoundly grateful to the reviewer for the positive evaluation:
“These composites not only exhibit superhardness and electrical conductivity but also
show potential for electromagnetic wave-absorbing applications”, and
recommendation for publication in Nature Communications. We greatly appreciate
these suggestions, which have been invaluable in improving the quality and clarity of
our work. We have carefully addressed all of your comments in a point-by-point manner
and revised the manuscript accordingly, as detailed below.

The authors should provide direct evidence to clarify the nature of the bonding at the
interface, determining the type of interaction—whether it is Van der Waals or covalent.
This clarification is crucial for offering a structural explanation for the superior
mechanical and microwave absorption performance.

the interfacial bonding between diamond and graphene is critical to understanding the
origin of the superior mechanical and microwave absorption performance. To address
this issue, we have added additional high-angle annular dark field scanning
transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) characterizations focusing on the
diamond-graphene interface (Fig. R1). Fig. R1a presents the HAADF-STEM image of
the sample synthesized at 7.0 GPa and 1300 °C, where diamond (D) and graphene (G)
nanodomains can be clearly distinguished. The magnified STEM images further reveal
an atomically coherent alignment at the interface—showing a correspondence between
the graphene and diamond layers. This observation provides direct structural evidence
that the composite is composed of nanoscale diamond and graphitic domains that are
interconnected via coherently bonded interfaces rather than simple Van der Waals
contact. Such atomic-level continuity suggests partial sp²-sp³ hybrid bonding across the

interface, which plays a critical role in ensuring mechanical integrity and facilitating
interfacial polarization and electron transport, thereby enhancing electromagnetic wave
absorption performance.

2. Given the authors' recent report on synthesizing similar composite Diaphene [PNAS,

Reply: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the
comparison with the Diaphene composite (PNAS, 2024, 121(9), e2316580121). We
have conducted a detailed comparison between the present DC composite and the
Diaphene material in terms of preparation methods, microstructural characteristics, and
mechanical properties, as summarized below.
Preparation methods: Unlike conventional high-pressure and high-temperature
(HPHT) conversions of sp² carbon to diamond, Diaphene was synthesized through the
partial graphitization of nanodiamond precursors under moderate HPHT conditions
(~12 GPa and 1300-1500 °C), enabling centimetre-scale synthesis in a large-volume
press. In contrast, our DC composites were prepared using a pre-graphitization strategy,
in which nanodiamond precursors were first annealed at 1200 °C in a vacuum to induce
16
controlled surface graphitization while preserving the sp3 diamond cores, followed by
HPHT treatment at ~7 GPa and 1100-1300 °C. This approach effectively reduces the
synthesis pressure and temperature while still enabling centimetre-scale fabrication in
a large-volume press.
Microstructural characteristics (Fig. R2): The Diaphene material exhibits a
bicontinuous nanoscale architecture consisting of 5-10 nm diamond grains
interpenetrated by curved few-layer graphene domains (typically ~5 layers),
interconnected through covalent sp²-sp³ interfaces that ensure mechanical and electrical
coupling. Similarly, the DC composites comprise multi-layer (~20 layers) graphene
domains uniformly embedded within nanodiamond matrices, with strong covalently
bonded interfaces that form a robust hybrid framework.
Mechanical properties (Fig. R3): The Diaphene exhibits a Vickers hardness of
42.5-55.8 GPa, and a fracture toughness of 10.8-19.8 MPa·m1/2, whereas our DC
composites show comparable values, with hardnesses of 41.9-51.7 GPa and fracture
toughnesses of 10.5-16.8 MPa·m1/2. The mechanical performance parity between DC
and Diaphene can be attributed to their similar microstructural compositions—
specifically, the coexistence of diamond and graphene components connected through
covalent sp²-sp³ bonding networks.

The superior oxidation resistance of DC-3 (1145 K) compared with natural
diamond, NPD, and Diaphene arises from both thermodynamic and kinetic stabilization
effects introduced by the diamond/graphene heterostructure. The interfacial sp³-sp²
covalent bonds reduce surface dangling bonds and lower the system’s Gibbs free energy,
thereby suppressing oxygen adsorption and increasing the oxidation activation energy.
Meanwhile, the dense graphene domains act as diffusion barriers that hinder oxygen
transport and delay carbon–oxygen bond formation. Additionally, charge redistribution
at the interface generates localized dipoles that stabilize surface electrons and suppress
defect-driven oxidation. These combined effects effectively inhibit lattice disorder and
carbon oxide formation, resulting in the remarkably high oxidation onset temperature
observed in DC-3.

2. The authors mention that the incoherent interface between diamond and
graphene enhances impedance matching, but they do not elaborate on the specific
mechanism by which the incoherent interface regulates the impedance matching
coefficient. What is the relationship between the structural features of the incoherent
interface (e.g., grain size of the ND, interface defect density, lattice mismatch) and the
impedance matching performance, and is there experimental or simulation
evidence to support this relationship? A theoretical simulation would be helpful to
elucidate the underline mechanism.
Reply: Thank you very much for your kind suggestions and corrections. To
address these issues, we have performed first principles calculations to elucidate their
influence and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the observed behavior.
To elucidate the role of interfacial defects, we constructed two types of interface
models between diamond and graphene—one incorporating vacancy defects and the
other defect-free. Calculations of their dielectric constants and impedance matching
coefficient for both models are presented in Figs. R2a-c. When the calculated dielectric
parameters were introduced into the impedance matching model, the interface with
defects yielded a matching coefficient closer to unity at a thickness of 1.0 mm. These
results suggest that the presence of vacancy defects at the diamond–graphene interface
enhances EWA by improving impedance matching.
To elucidate the effect of grain size on the impedance matching behavior, we
constructed interfacial models with varying grain sizes. The models were systematically
labeled size-1, size-2, and size-3 to denote a progressive increase in grain size. The
theoretically derived complex dielectric constants are presented in Figs. R2d-i.
Below 12 GHz, size-3 exhibits a superior dielectric constant (real part), indicating strong
charge storage capability. But beyond 12 GHz, its permittivity drops sharply, falling
below that of both size-1 and size-2. Fig. R2h presents the imaginary component of the
dielectric constant for three models with varying sizes at 1.0 mm, showing a gradual
increase in dielectric loss with increasing size. However, comparison of their
impedance matching coefficients (Fig. R2i) reveals that smaller-sized models exhibit
superior impedance matching, indicating that reduced grain size facilitates more
efficient penetration and attenuation of electromagnetic waves within the material.

than 10⁻⁶ A/cm², indicating good corrosion resistance. But the manuscript does not
explain why the corrosion resistance of DC-1 (with higher sp³ content) is slightly better
than that of DC-2 and DC-3, as suggested by the Nyquist plots. What is the intrinsic
relationship between sp³/sp² content and the corrosion resistance mechanism of the
composites?
Reply: Thank you for your insightful comment. The corrosion resistance of the
DC composites is intrinsically governed by the ratio and distribution of sp³ and sp²
carbon domains, which jointly determine the chemical stability and electrochemical
activity of the material. The sp³-bonded diamond phase provides a chemically inert
framework with high bond energy and low surface reactivity, acting as a barrier against
oxidative and electrochemical attack. In contrast, sp²-bonded graphene domains possess
higher electrical conductivity and facilitate charge transfer at the solid–liquid interface,
but their π-bonded structure is more susceptible to oxidation and electron-induced
corrosion. Therefore, the corrosion behavior arises from a delicate balance: a higher sp³
fraction enhances chemical inertness and passivation stability, while moderate sp²
incorporation improves charge dissipation and reduces local potential gradients that can
initiate pitting. Moreover, the covalently bonded sp²-sp³ interfaces suppress defect
formation and inhibit electrolyte penetration, providing synergistic protection.
Consequently, the optimized sp³-sp² hybrid architecture yields superior corrosion
resistance by combining the chemical stability of diamond with the electronic buffering
capability of graphene.
We have added the corresponding discussions in the revised manuscript: “This
behavior correlates directly with the sp³/sp² ratio: the diamond matrix supplies chemical
inertness, while sp2 domains promote charge delocalization and minimize local
potential gradients. Excessive sp², however, increases surface reactivity, underscoring
the need for an optimized hybrid ratio. Thus, an optimal balance between the two
ensures both structural stability and electronic equilibrium at the interface22, effectively
improving corrosion resistance through synergistic chemical passivation and charge
delocalization.” (Page 18, Lines 5-10)

change of dielectric parameters (ε', ε'') with temperature. What are the variations of

Reply: Thank you for your insightful comment. We apologize for the earlier

permeability at different high temperatures are shown in Fig. R4. Both ε' and ε'' decrease

magnetic permeability, owing to its intrinsically low magnitude, shows only a minor
thermal dependence.

to get the reflection loss plot of 2D based on the measured electromagnetic parameters
(Fig. R5). As the temperature increases, the optimal absorption performance gradually
shifts toward larger thicknesses, indicating that the thickness of the absorber plays a
crucial role in determining electromagnetic wave attenuation. To enable a consistent
comparison, we analyzed the absorption bandwidths at different temperatures at a fixed
thickness of 3.2 mm. Under this condition, the absorption bandwidth was found to

thickness, the bandwidth gradually narrows35.” (Page 18, Lines 13-17)

6. The manuscript proposes that the heterostructure design of diamond-graphene
composites provides a new strategy for multifunctional electromagnetic wave
absorbing materials, but it does not discuss the scalability and cost of the moderate
high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) synthesis method. What challenges exist
in scaling up the HPHT preparation process for industrial production, and are there
potential improvements to reduce the synthesis cost while maintaining material
performance?
Reply: Thank you for this valuable comment. We agree that the scalability and
cost of the HPHT method are important considerations for practical application. While
our study focuses primarily on revealing the structure-property relationship in diamond-
graphene heterostructures, we acknowledge that several challenges remain in scaling
up the HPHT process for industrial production.
HPHT synthesis requires ultra-high pressure and high temperature. These systems
are expensive, energy intensive, and currently limited to small batch sizes. In addition,
high-strength anvils, heating elements, and pressure medium materials degrade under
extreme conditions and require frequent replacement, increasing production costs.
Several potential strategies may help improve scalability and reduce cost.
Optimizing catalysts or introducing pre-bonded nanodiamond-graphene intermediates
31
may reduce the required P-T conditions while still forming stable heterostructures. Also,
combining HPHT with techniques such as spark plasma sintering (SPS) or hot pressing
under moderate pressure may lower energy consumption and enable near-net-shape
fabrication.

synthesis reliably produces covalently bonded sp³-sp² interfaces and high-performance
composites, scale-up remains limited by the requirements of ultra-high pressure, high
temperature, and high energy consumption. Strategies to reduce cost and improve
throughput include tailoring precursor chemistry to lower transformation thresholds,
adopting spark plasma sintering (SPS)40 or hot-pressing, and exploring hybrid HPHT-
SPS approaches. In addition, emerging metal-catalyzed pathways, such as liquid Ga-,
Ni-, or Cu-mediated formation of sp³-sp² interfaces41-46 offer promising alternative
routes to large-scale production of covalently integrated carbon heterostructures.”
(Page 18, Lines 18-22; Page 19, Lines 1-3)
